newsitem.title: UK: London gold prices slumps ahead of U.S. holiday.
newsitem.headline: London gold prices slumps ahead of U.S. holiday.

text.p: The gold price slumped to its lowest fixing since January 9, 1995 on Tuesday afternoon as aftershocks from an overnight New York sell-off continued to shake the market, dealers said.
The fixing at $373.50 per ounce was a dollar down on the morning setting, which itself compared with $375.10 and $375.40 recorded on Monday, when the morning fix was the lowest since March 2, 1995.
"Everybody is squaring up ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday in the U.S. Why be long at a time like this?" one dealer said.
Market confidence had been wobbling since the failure earlier this month of attempts to break out and above the $375-$385 corset gold had occupied since early September.

Comments by International Monetary Fund (IMF) treasurer David Williams on the IMF's contingency plan to sell five million ounces of gold to help the world's poorest nations at a conference in London last week damaged residual confidence.
Also last week, Swiss National Bank (SNB) director Peter Klauser said political pressure could lead the SNB to take a more pro-active approach to its reserves, including gold.
The SNB's gold reserves are stable at about 2,600 tonnes. and are valued at an official gold price at 4,595.75 Swiss francs per kilo.
Klauser noted that other central banks had managed their gold pro-actively through selling part of their holding or mobilising some of them through swaps, lending or options.
In the past Swiss central bankers have indicated that policy on gold could be adjusted.

In April the then outgoing SNB president Markus Lusser called on parliament to drop a legal requirement that the SNB keep physical gold reserves to support the Swiss franc and instead allow the bank to use currency reserves as a provision.
Referring to the latest comments, CRU International metals analayst Tony Warwick-Ching said, "I don't think for a minute that it means that they're going to sell anything.
"It just means they're recognising what everyone else has recognised, that even if you have enough gold, there is no point in maintaining a direct cover to the currency."

Warwick-Ching added, "There's no reason why the market should react to this news. But the bullion market is so sensitised to this sort of thing...there's so much talk of what central banks might or might not do."
The highly conservative nature of the SNB had added to the significance of the officials' thoughts, analyst said.

"This is a role model for a central banker saying things can be different, things can be more realistic. Once you start being realistic about gold, it's negative," said Union Bank of Switzerland bullion analyst Andy Smith.
"It has to go through a very intricate democratic process -- parliament and a referendum -- and 1998 is the first time something like this could happen," he added.

"The bulls have been arguing for years and years that estabilished, traditional central banks would never think about mobilising gold. Here we have the most traditional and established central bank saying it might do exactly that," Smith added.
